name: Hana Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four and in the parlour by five, because I manage the herd and the crops at Ridgeway, which is a cooperative farm owned by about forty families in the valley. We milk a hundred and eighty cows twice a day, grow barley and grass on the rest, and I've got five people working with me. I still write everything in a paper diary with a rubber band round it, which drives the co-op office mad. The best bit is calving at night when it goes right, and the worst bit is the paperwork and the milk price letter every month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work most closely with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Deepak, my head tractor man, who's been there longer than me and won't let anyone else touch the baler. And Ruth, who's twenty and the best young stockperson I've seen in years. My partner Sam works on the council road crew, so between us we pay the mortgage on a terrace house in the village, and Lia and Tomas get the bus to school from the end of our lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. I'd say it at the union branch meeting and to the co-op board, who've been sent three glossy brochures about robot milkers this year. Cows don't care about hype, and neither does the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays what it is, which is hard but mine. The milk price is still the thing that keeps me up, not computers. If anything, I'd be relieved I never bothered learning any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as we are, really. I'd push the board to spend the money they'd set aside for a robot trial on a second calving pen and a pay rise for Ruth instead. I'd keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage when the barley sells, like we always do in September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the board has brochures. Who brings those in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machinery dealer from town, and a young lad on the board who reads farming magazines on his phone. I don't blame him, he's keen. I blame the companies who sell it as the answer to everything, when the real answer is a fair milk price and enough hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So in this picture, what does a normal Tuesday look like a year from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as today. Five o'clock milking, Deepak complaining about the baler, me shouting at the printer in the office. Maybe the co-op office does the milk records quicker with some computer thing, and that's fine by me as long as I never have to touch it.

S0.say: I'd tell the union branch and the co-op board that I said so all along, and that the robot milker brochures can go in the recycling. Cows and weather don't care about hype.
S0.think: My job stays hard but mine, and the milk price stays the real worry. I'm privately relieved I never had to learn any of the new tools.
S0.do: Keeps running the herd as now and pushes the board to spend the robot trial money on a second calving pen and a raise for Ruth. Keeps paying a little extra off the mortgage each September when the barley sells.
S0.quote: Cows don't care about hype, and neither does the weather.
S0.fieldNote: Hana is proud of doing things on paper and sees the robot brochures as a sales push rather than a real need. Her worry is the milk price and staffing, not technology. She points blame at the companies selling the kit, not at the keen young board member.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the branch that we need a deal before any of this comes in. If robots are milking, the workers who stay should get trained and paid properly, and the ones who go should get something decent. I'd probably post that in the farmworkers' group too, which is about the only online thing I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the board would buy two robot milkers within three years, and the parlour job is what goes. That's my job, mostly, and Ruth's. I'd be the one they keep to watch the screens, and I'd be bad at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting and get the union to write a proper agreement with the co-op about how many jobs stay. I'd stop the extra mortgage payments and keep that money in the bank instead, maybe three or four hundred a month. And I'd make Ruth go on the robot course, even if I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing a storm on the forecast for next week. You get the hay in, but you keep looking at the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd send Ruth on the course but not go yourself. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because she's twenty and she'll still be farming in 2060. I'm forty-three and I've got a way of doing things that works. I know that sounds stubborn. Sam says it's stubborn. But I'd rather be the best at the old way than average at the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lia and Tomas about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the cows still need someone who knows them. Lia wants to be a vet, and I'd tell her to keep going with that. Tomas just wants to drive the tractor, and I don't know what I'd tell him.

S1.say: I'd tell the union branch and the farmworkers' online group that we need a written deal before robots come in. People who stay should be trained and paid properly, and people who go should get a fair settlement.
S1.think: I think the board would buy robot milkers within three years and the parlour work, which is most of my job and Ruth's, would go. I'd be kept on to watch screens and I'd be bad at it.
S1.do: Goes to every union branch meeting to press for a jobs agreement with the co-op. Stops overpaying the mortgage and keeps three or four hundred a month in savings, and sends young Ruth on the robot training instead of going herself.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm on next week's forecast.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the best at the old way than average at the new one.
S1.fieldNote: Hana sees the threat clearly and answers it with organising rather than retraining. She admits her own stubbornness when asked, and she'd protect the younger worker's future while declining to change herself. Her reply about Tomas trailed off in a way that felt more honest than anything else she said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the branch: this is the companies grabbing everything before anyone can write a rule. I'd want the government to stop it, or at least slow it down, and I'd say that on the farmworkers' group and at the pub. Two years is nothing on a farm. One barley crop to the next is a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I think I'm finished as a farm manager. A co-op of forty families will buy whatever's cheapest, because they've got their own mortgages. If a robot can calve a heifer at two in the morning, they don't need me. I've never even used one of those chat programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop every spend that isn't food, the mortgage or the kids. No holiday, no new car, Tomas's football camp gets cut. I'd go to the council with the union and push for a fund for farm workers, and I'd ask Sam whether the road crew is safe, because that might be what holds us up. Once it arrives, I'd probably look for anything going, even if it's driving for the council like Sam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. My stomach drops. I'd be up at night going through the numbers on the back of the diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sam's job might hold you up. How long could your savings carry you if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four months, maybe five if we're really tight. The mortgage is the big one, eight hundred and forty a month. After that it's my mum's spare room, and I really don't want to be forty-four and living at my mum's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two years change, compared with having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With two years I can't retrain for anything, I can barely get through one harvest and a winter of calving. The time is the whole problem. If you gave me ten years I'd at least have a fight, but two years is just watching it happen.

S2.say: I'd say at the branch, at the pub and online that the companies are grabbing everything before anyone can write a rule. I'd call for the government to stop it or slow it right down.
S2.think: I think I'm finished as a farm manager, because a co-op of families with their own mortgages will buy whatever is cheapest. I've never even used a chat program, so I'd be starting from nothing.
S2.do: Cuts every spend except food, the mortgage and the children, including Tomas's football camp and the holiday. Pushes the council with the union for a fund for farm workers, and once it arrives looks for any work going, such as the council road crew.
S2.feel: Frightened, and up at night doing sums on the back of her diary.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing on a farm. One barley crop to the next is a year.
S2.fieldNote: The short warning time is what breaks her confidence: she measures time in harvests and calvings. She has four or five months of savings against an 840-a-month mortgage and names her mother's spare room as the fallback. Her anger is aimed at the companies and at missing rules, not at the co-op families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the fast one, but I'd say we've got time to do something about it, so let's do it. I'd want the union pushing for a law that farms using robots pay into a fund for the workers they replace. I'd probably write a letter to the paper, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'm forty-eight when it lands. That's still eighteen years from the pension. I think I'd be out of work and too old to start again, and too young to stop. That's the worst age for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd save every penny I could, maybe five hundred a month if we cut the car loan early. I'd be at every meeting, and I'd put my name forward for branch secretary. Somewhere in year three I'd probably have to look at something else, maybe teaching at the agricultural college, if they still need people to teach anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I can see it coming, but it sits on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. With five years' warning, would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say no. But if the college job is the plan, I suppose I'd have to learn enough not to look like a fool in front of the students. Ruth could show me. That's a strange thought, Ruth teaching me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most at Ridgeway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deepak. He's fifty-six, he doesn't read well, and the baler is his whole pride. He'd have nothing. I'd want the co-op to keep him on for as long as there was anything a person could do, even if it's just walking the hedges.

S3.say: I'd tell people we have time to act, so we should, starting with a law making farms that use robots pay into a fund for the workers they replace. I'd even write to the local paper for the first time.
S3.think: Five years means I'd be forty-eight when it lands, too old to start again and too young to stop. I think that's the worst possible age to lose the job.
S3.do: Saves around five hundred a month by paying off the car loan early, and stands for union branch secretary. Around year three looks at teaching at the agricultural college, and reluctantly asks Ruth to show her the AI tools.
S3.feel: Anxious, with a weight on her chest, but not panicked because she can see it coming.
S3.quote: I'd be out of work and too old to start again, and too young to stop.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Hana room to organise but she still sees no place for herself on a farm. She softens on learning AI only when it serves a fallback teaching job, and the idea of the young worker teaching her clearly unsettled her. Her first worry for others was Deepak, an older worker with fewer options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, and if we don't, it's a choice. I'd say that loudly at the branch and to our MP. The farms can have their robots, but the people who built those farms need a share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me fifty-three, and I think I'd still be useful for a good part of it. The robots would come in bit by bit, and the co-op would need someone who knows the land and the herd to set them up right. I just don't believe I'd be that person, because I'd have refused to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal for the first couple of years and watch what the bigger farms do. I'd keep saving, and I'd push the union to get retraining money for older workers written in early. If by year five the robots were real, I'd do the college teaching course part-time, and Lia would be through school by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious. Less sharp, more like a dull ache you live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is enough to do it properly. Is it enough for you to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if I'm honest. That's the annoying part. With ten years I can't really hide behind 'there's no time'. I'd have to admit it's me not wanting to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Tomas to hear from you about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That his mum fought for the people on the farm, not just for herself. And that he should learn whatever the machines can't do, though I couldn't tell him what that is.

S4.say: I'd tell the union branch and our MP that ten years is enough to do this fairly, and failing would be a choice. The people who built the farms deserve a share of what the robots earn.
S4.think: At fifty-three I'd probably still be useful while the robots come in bit by bit. But I doubt I'd be the one setting them up, because I'd have refused to learn.
S4.do: Keeps working as normal for the first two years while watching the bigger farms, and keeps saving. Pushes the union to get retraining money for older workers agreed early, and starts a part-time college teaching course around year five.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but as a dull ache rather than a sharp fear.
S4.quote: With ten years I can't really hide behind 'there's no time'. I'd have to admit it's me not wanting to.
S4.fieldNote: More time eased the panic but exposed her own reluctance, which she named herself without being pushed. Her plan is still collective first and personal change later. What she wants Tomas to remember is that she fought for others.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. What would help is a fund that farms pay into when they bring robots in, so people like Deepak and me get paid while we find something else. And a union that's at the table before the brochures arrive, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but someone has to notice when a cow's off her feed before the numbers show it. I hope whoever's watching the robots still walks the shed at night.

headlineQuote: Someone has to notice when a cow's off her feed before the numbers show it.
portrait: Hana Costa is 43 and manages the dairy herd and barley at Ridgeway, a cooperative farm owned by forty valley families, with a team of five. She keeps her records in a paper diary, has never used an AI tool, and is a committed union member who blames the companies selling the kit rather than the farmers buying it. She shrugs off the plateau, organises for a jobs deal under steady change, and is frightened by two-year AGI because her savings last four or five months against an 840-a-month mortgage. With five or ten years she would save, stand for union office and edge towards teaching at the agricultural college, while admitting that the real obstacle is her own reluctance to learn.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years is barely one harvest and a winter of calving, with no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A fund that farms pay into when they bring in robots, so displaced workers are paid while they find something else, and a union seat at the table before the decisions are made.
